While looking into that, I found a publishing tool used overseas called Substack. It combines a blog and a newsletter, is free to start, and allows for paid distribution. In this article, I will summarize the differences from note, its weaknesses, and how to get started. This content was originally organized around May 2026.

It started in 2017, and writers, journalists, and creators overseas have been migrating to it. It is not designed for viral spread; it has a strong character as a place to connect directly with people who read your work.

Since it is a service from overseas, the current situation is that there are still few Japanese writers and readers. You can hardly expect the kind of traffic where people browsing the platform find you on their own, as they do on note. You will be starting with the premise of bringing readers from SNS or existing blogs. Honestly, this is the easiest place to stumble.

The settings screen and management screen are basically all in English. However, since the number of buttons to press is small, using browser translation is usually sufficient. You can write the body text in Japanese, and you can also distribute it in Japanese.

Since it is automatically delivered to those who have registered when you publish, it will not be swept away and disappear in a timeline. It is also appreciated by those who continue to use it that it is unlikely to suddenly become unviewable due to specification changes, unlike SNS.

You can switch between free and paid articles, and it supports monthly and annual billing. Since payments are processed via Stripe (an overseas payment service), you do not need to build the mechanism yourself.

After that, just write an article and hit the publish button. It does not matter if you have zero registered readers. You can gradually invite people from social media or your existing blog as you write.

One hour later, the setup was complete. Everything from the publication name, pricing, payment registration, the welcome email sent to readers, to the bio page was done. After that, I published the first post and have already scheduled the second one.
In both cases, approximately 84% to 86% remains in your hand.

Another feature Substack has is a "Founding Member" tier. This is a system where readers decide for themselves to pay an amount higher than the annual subscription price. It is a tier for readers who want to support you, and it can be used in a way similar to the support feature on note.

Third, the email address to register with. It is safer to avoid addresses provided by your company or a contractor. If the contract ends, you may lose access to the address, which could prevent you from logging into your account.

Email addresses are assets for the future

Those who have read this far might be somewhat drawn to Substack's characteristics of "delivering slowly" and "connecting deeply with readers." But there is one more point that I think is important. That is, the email addresses of your subscribers remain in your own hands.

But Substack is different. The email addresses of people who subscribe remain as your own assets. For example, if something happens to Substack and you decide to move to another newsletter service, you can take your subscriber list with you.
